opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the thing that got us excited was that the embedding wasn't just good at the task we trained it on. We trained a graph neural network to take a molecule's structure and predict how it smells, using descriptors like "fruity," "garlicky," "woody." And it did that well. But when we looked inside, at the space the network had learned just before the output layer, it had real structure.

Molecules that smell alike sat close together, even when their chemical structures looked quite different. And the broad organization of that space made sense to people who smell things for a living. You'd see neighborhoods for things like meaty or alliaceous odors, floral regions, and so on, with gradients between them. It looked like a map, not just a classifier's internal bookkeeping.

The real test was whether it generalized beyond the labels we gave it. We used it for tasks it was never trained on: predicting odor similarity between pairs of molecules, and predicting the odor characteristics of molecules that weren't in our training data. It did well on those, which told us it had learned something about the underlying perceptual space, not just memorized a lookup table.

Then we tested it against people. We ran a prospective study with trained panelists who rated new molecules that neither the model nor the panelists had seen before. The model's predictions were, on average, closer to the panel consensus than a typical individual panelist was. That was the moment it stopped feeling like a nice machine learning result and started feeling like a tool for understanding perception.

There's also a deeper reason it made sense to call it a map. Color has a well-understood space, organized by wavelength and the cones in your eye. Sound has frequency. Smell has never had that. There's no obvious physical axis, because the inputs are molecules with incredibly varied structures, and we have hundreds of receptor types. So for a long time people weren't sure a coherent, low-dimensional perceptual map of smell even existed. Seeing the network converge on one that matched human judgment, and that we could navigate and make predictions with, suggested that a map is there, and that we can learn it from data.

r001.rationale: The response describes a structured embedding with odor neighborhoods and gradients, calls it a map, and cites successful predictions on untrained tasks as evidence it can predict smell.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the heart of it. When we trained the graph neural network on molecules, the task we gave it was pretty narrow: here's a molecular structure, predict which of these human-labeled odor descriptors apply to it. Floral, fruity, sulfurous, that kind of thing. And the model got good at that task, which was nice, but the thing that got me genuinely excited was what happened in the layer right before the output.

That penultimate layer is an embedding, a vector of a couple hundred numbers for every molecule. The network isn't told anything about what those dimensions should mean. It just has to organize molecules in a way that makes the prediction task solvable. And when we looked at that space, we saw structure that nobody had put in. Molecules that smell similar were clustered together, which you'd expect to some extent. But the clusters themselves were arranged in ways that mirrored how perfumers and flavor chemists already think about odor. The fruity region sat next to the floral region, the meaty and sulfurous stuff was off on its own side, and inside the fruity cluster you could find sub-neighborhoods for things like apple or citrus. It looked like a map, and a map that agreed with human intuition that had been built up over a century of practice.

The reason that mattered to me is that smell has never had a map. Vision has color space. We know that any color you can see can be described with three numbers, and we know why, because we understand the receptors. Audition has frequency. You can lay sound out along a single axis and the structure is right there. Olfaction has nothing like that. There are around four hundred receptor types in humans, the relationship between molecular structure and perception is famously messy, and the best anyone had were these hand-drawn odor wheels that are useful but aren't grounded in anything quantitative. Two molecules that look almost identical on paper can smell completely different, and two that look nothing alike can smell the same. So the field had sort of given up on there being a principled coordinate system.

What the embedding suggested was that maybe there is one, and we just hadn't been able to compute it. The model had to compress all this structural information down into something predictive of perception, and in doing so it seemed to have found a representation where distance meant something about smell. That's a strong claim, so the thing we immediately did was try to break it. We asked, does this map predict things it wasn't trained on? Can it predict receptor activation? Can it predict odor intensity, or which molecules will smell similar to a panel of people it has never seen? And when it generalized to those out-of-distribution questions better than the standard chemistry descriptors did, that's when I started to think this wasn't just a useful classifier. It looked like a candidate for the thing the field had been missing, a principal odor map, in the same way we have a color space.

I want to be careful about it, because an embedding is just a tool, and it's the validation that makes it a map. But the fact that an optimization process with no knowledge of perfumery rediscovered the structure of perfumery was the signal that we were onto something real.

r001.rationale: The response describes the embedding as an organized space where distance reflects smell, and says its structure and predictive generalization suggest it could be a principled odor map.

astra-6.text:
What was exciting was that we trained the network to take a molecule’s structure and predict how it smells. To do that, it builds an internal representation—an embedding—and we started asking whether the organization of that space reflected something meaningful about smell.

Molecules that look similar chemically don’t necessarily smell similar, and molecules that look quite different can smell alike. So a useful map has to capture something beyond structural similarity. In the embedding, we were seeing molecules organize according to their odor character: things that smell similar were close together.

That suggested the network was learning more than a collection of separate labels. It might be learning a shared representation of smell, where relationships between odors are captured by relationships between points. That’s what made it promising as a map—and gave us something we could test on molecules the model hadn’t seen before.

r001.rationale: It says molecules organize by odor character in the embedding, with similar-smelling molecules close together, and describes odor relationships as relationships between points. Because the network predicts smell from molecular structure and this organization could be tested on unseen molecules, the embedding is presented as a continuous predictive map.

sol-6.1.text:
What was striking was that we trained this network to predict how a molecule smells from its structure, and in doing that, it had to build an internal representation of those molecules. We started asking whether that representation captured something more general about smell than just the labels we'd trained it on.

If you look at chemical structure alone, two molecules can look very similar and smell completely different. And two molecules that look quite different can smell similar. So a useful map of smell has to bring together molecules that are perceptually similar, even when their chemistry isn't obviously similar.

We saw evidence of that in the embedding: molecules with similar odor descriptions tended to be near one another. That suggested the network was learning some of the organization of olfactory perception. It wasn't proof that we'd solved smell, but it gave us a very concrete hypothesis to test: could distances in this space tell us how a new molecule would smell to a person?

r001.rationale: The response says odor-similar molecules clustered in the embedding and proposes using distances in that space to predict how a new molecule would smell, presenting the embedding as a predictive map of smell.
